title: Incense Offering Ritual
summary: You've lit the incense, but you mustn't blow it out with your mouth -- and the first deity you greet on entering isn't the main god, but Tiangong, the Jade Emperor. Offering incense looks simple, yet the fine points are many. A single stick of incense is the line of communication between worshipper and deity, and this guide walks you through how to offer it and how to pray.
content:
A lit stick of incense pinched between your fingers -- who do you bow to first? Can you blow it out with your mouth? Standing before the burner, many people are only half sure. A stick of pure incense is the thread that ties worshipper to deity, and behind so simple an act lies a whole set of etiquette.

【Step 1: Cleanse Your Hands and Take the Incense】
Before entering, wash your hands to purify yourself -- a mark of respect for the deity. Take one stick, or three (temples differ, and in recent years many encourage a single "incense of the heart" for the environment). Light it at the candle flame, and if a flame flares up, never blow it out with your mouth -- this is the most basic taboo. Shake it gently or fan it out with your hand, and let the thin curl of blue smoke rise.

【Step 2: Worship Tiangong】
Whatever temple you enter, the first to receive your worship is usually not the main deity in the hall but "Tiangong" -- the Jade Emperor. Face outward (or toward the Tiangong censer), hold the incense in both hands above your head, about eyebrow height, and silently recite your name, lunar birthday, address, and the purpose and wish that bring you today. Say it clearly and fully, so the deity knows who is asking and for what. Then bow three times.

【Step 3: Worship the Main Deity】
Turn to face the main deity in the central hall, again raise the incense above your head in both hands, silently recite your name and wish once more, and bow three times. If there's something special on your mind, tell it quietly within -- "sincerity brings a response" (xin cheng ze ling) is the single most central saying in Taiwanese folk belief.

【Step 4: Plant the Incense】
After worshipping, place the incense in the burner. Tradition favors the left hand (folk belief holds the left to be the "clean hand"). Set it in straight, not leaning or toppled. If the temple has several burners, plant one in each in the order "outer to inner, center to side." Some temples cap their burners or limit where incense may go -- just follow the temple's guidance.

【Step 5: Worship the Attendant Deities in Turn】
Once you've worshipped the main deity, don't rush off; go on to the attendant deities in the side halls and rear hall, in the order "dragon side first (the deity's left, as you face it), then tiger side (the right)." Worshipping only the main deity while neglecting the rest is seen as less than reverent.

【Things to Note】
- When holding incense in both hands, keep the burning tip pointed up, never down.
- Stay quiet while worshipping; no horseplay or noise.
- Many temples now promote "palms pressed together" in place of holding incense -- Xingtian Temple, for instance, banned incense entirely from 2014, switching to worship with joined palms and a silent inward prayer, which devotees consider every bit as sincere and effective.
- On your first visit to a temple, it helps to read the worship notice at the gate, or ask a temple volunteer.

title: Burning Joss Paper
summary: Gold paper for the gods, silver paper for the ancestors, and never the two confused -- this is the most basic rule of burning joss paper. In the drifting ash, Taiwanese people convey their hearts to gods and ancestors, and this old tradition is now finding a new balance between environmental care and faith.
content:
Before the furnace, sheet after sheet of paper money is fed into the fire, the flames lighting the faces around it -- one of the most emblematic sights on any Taiwanese temple plaza. Burning joss paper is a way of conveying the heart to gods and ancestors, and the one rule you must never get wrong lies in the single character's difference between "gold" and "silver."

【Gold Paper vs. Silver Paper】
The difference between gold and silver paper is the most basic, and most important, rule:
- Gold paper (gilded with gold foil) is strictly for the gods. Common kinds include "Tiangong Gold" (for the Jade Emperor, the highest grade, with the largest and finest foil), "Shou Gold" (for deities in general, the most used), "Yi Gold" (for general worship), "Fu Gold" (for the Earth God, small in denomination but full of sincerity), and "Pen Gold" (large denomination, for major ceremonies). Different deities take different grades, and the top-ranking Tiangong Gold must not be offered to ordinary deities.
- Silver paper (with silver foil) is for ancestors and the "good brothers" (wandering spirits). Common kinds include "Big Silver" (for ancestors, the larger grade), "Small Silver" (for the good brothers, the smallest), "Lotus Silver" (for delivering souls, often folded into lotuses), and "Rebirth Money" (printed with Buddhist scripture, for salvation). Silver paper must never be offered to the gods, nor gold paper to the good brothers -- one of the most basic taboos in Taiwanese folk belief.

【How to Burn It, and What to Avoid】
Burning gold paper usually comes as the last step of the whole worship. First fold each sheet in half (turning the flat paper into the shape of an ingot), then place it reverently into the furnace to burn. A few key points:
- The order is gold first, then silver -- and gold and silver must never be burned together; mixing them is thought disrespectful to both gods and ancestors.
- Don't tread on scattered ash while it burns, and don't leave partway through; wait until the money has burned completely.
- Don't toss the paper in carelessly or leave it half-burned -- both are seen as irreverent to the gods.
- Some worshippers write their name on the paper, so the gods or ancestors know whose offering it is.

【Special Papers and Foldings】
- Treasury-Replenishing Gold: burned to replenish one's personal "wealth treasury," often at wealth-god temples. Some temples add a written "petition" (shuwen) to burn alongside, stating the reason and the wish.
- Tai Sui Gold: burned when you clash with Tai Sui, to pray for calamity to disperse and a safe passage through the year.
- Rebirth Lotus: silver paper folded sheet by sheet into a lotus, the most heartfelt way to deliver the departed. Folding lotuses is painstaking work -- each bloom takes a dozen or more sheets, layered up, symbolizing new life for the departed upon the lotus. At Taiwanese funerals, family and friends often sit together folding lotuses, a way of both mourning the dead and mending their own grief.

【The Modern Green Trend】
As environmental awareness has grown, many temples now offer alternatives:
- "Rice for Gold": putting the money you'd have spent on paper toward rice donated to social-welfare groups.
- "Merit for Gold": donating to good causes instead of burning, dedicating the merit to gods or ancestors.
- "Reduced Burning": burning only a small amount of paper as a token of the heart.
- Xingtian Temple went furthest, becoming the first to ban joss-paper burning outright in favor of "joined palms, sincere heart."
- Some temples have installed "eco furnaces" fitted with air filtration and ash collection to lessen the impact.
More and more people accept that "sincerity brings a response" -- what matters is the respect and the heart, not how much paper is burned. This old tradition is slowly finding a new balance between the environment and faith.

title: Preparing Offerings
summary: For Wenchang Dijun, the god of scholars, you offer scallions and celery; Tiger Lord loves raw eggs; and you must never set a custard apple before the Buddha. Offerings are a worshipper's gift of the heart, but what may be offered and what is taboo each follow their own rules -- learn them, and every visit becomes respectful and fitting.
content:
Students worshipping Wenchang Dijun lay out scallions, celery, and radish; for Tiger Lord you bring raw eggs; but set a custard apple before the Buddha and you've committed a real discourtesy. Offerings are a worshipper's gift of the heart, yet Taiwanese folk custom keeps a fine set of rules about what may be offered and what is taboo.

【Basic Offerings】
- Fresh flowers: for purity and dignity, chrysanthemums and lilies are the most common; for the Buddha, lotus is best. Flowers must be fresh and whole -- nothing wilted goes on the altar.
- Fruit (the "four fruits"): "four fruits" doesn't mean four kinds, but "fruits of the four seasons." Usually you offer an odd number of kinds (three or five), an odd number of each. Wash and dry the fruit; nothing worm-eaten or spoiled.
- Tea and wine: tea or rice wine is offered to the deities, usually three cups. Buddhist temples generally use only plain water or tea, no wine.
- Cakes: for sweetness and good fortune -- "nian gao" (sticky, to "hold on to money"), "fa gao" (prosperity cake), and "ang ku kueh" (red tortoise cake, for longevity), each with its lucky meaning.

【The Three and Five Offerings】
- Three offerings (san sheng): pork (belly pork with the skin on), a whole chicken, and a whole fish -- the most formal set for worshipping the gods.
- Five offerings (wu sheng): the three offerings plus duck and shrimp (or crab), a higher grade, used for occasions like the Jade Emperor's birthday or a temple's opening.
- Vegetarian three offerings: mock versions made of tofu, wheat gluten, and vegetarian chicken, for Buddhist deities or those who take no meat.

【What Particular Deities Like】
- The Wealth God: loves sweets -- candy, peanut brittle, and cakes; adding peanuts (for "long life") and mochi (to "hold on to money") is better still.
- Tiger Lord: likes raw eggs and raw meat -- being an animal deity, his offerings should be "raw," and some worshippers even offer raw pig liver.
- The Earth God (Bogong): the most down-to-earth of deities, fond of peanuts (tudou, for "long life") and mochi (to hold on to wealth and blessings).
- Yue Lao: fresh flowers and wedding candy; those seeking a match also bring red thread.
- Wenchang Dijun: students offer scallions (for cleverness), celery (for diligence), garlic (for reckoning), radish (for good luck), and zongzi and buns (for "passing the exam").
- Mazu: peach-shaped longevity buns, longevity noodles, and red tortoise cake, offered in gratitude to this motherly deity.

【Offering Taboos】
- Guava: full of seeds and hard to digest, it was thought "unclean" by the ancients and unfit for the gods.
- Tomato: for the same reason as guava, also counted an unclean fruit.
- Custard apple (sakya): its name matches "Shakyamuni," so offering it to the Buddha is deemed a grave irreverence.
- Plum: folk belief says the Taoist founder Laozi was surnamed Li ("plum"), so offering plums to worship is as good as "eating Laozi."
- Water spinach (hollow-heart vegetable): its "hollow heart" suggests a lack of sincere heart.
- Pineapple ("ong lai," prosperity comes), apple ("peace"), and orange ("good luck"): the most welcome auspicious offerings.

【Arranging the Offerings】
Set the offerings neatly on the altar table, fruit and cakes before the deity, and with the three offerings, the chicken's head facing the deity. The cups of tea and wine go in front of the offerings. Afterward you may take the offerings home to eat -- "eating peace," as it's called -- a way of taking the deity's blessing home with you.

title: Lighting Beacon Lamps
summary: A whole wall of thousands of tiny lamps, each inscribed with a person's name, burning day and night -- these are the bright lamps (guangming deng) of the temple. To light one is to light your own natal star, brightening the road ahead and dispelling the dark, one of the most important acts of faith as Taiwanese people welcome the New Year.
content:
Step into a temple's Hall of Light and you'll find a whole wall -- sometimes a towering lamp-pagoda -- packed with thousands of tiny lamps, each bearing a person's name, never going dark. These are the bright lamps. Every year before Lunar New Year the queues to register stretch long, because lighting a lamp is one of the most important acts of faith by which Taiwanese people greet the New Year.

【Meaning and Origin】
The bright lamp stands for the "yuanchen" -- each person's natal star. Folk belief holds that everyone has a star of their own in the heavens; when its light dims, fortune sinks and the road ahead grows unclear. To light a bright lamp is to rekindle that natal star, so the way forward shines and fortune flows. The custom blends the Taoist idea of the "natal lamp" with the Buddhist tradition of "lighting lamps as an offering to the Buddha," forming a lamp-lighting culture distinct to Taiwan. Each little lamp, name-inscribed and burning day and night, stands for the deity's constant watch.

【Types and Purposes】
Taiwanese temples offer many kinds of lamp, each for a different wish:
- Bright Lamp: the most common, for safety and a bright road ahead; suited to everyone, the most basic and popular choice.
- Tai Sui Lamp: a must for those whose zodiac clashes with the year's Tai Sui (direct or partial), to pray for calamity to disperse and a safe passage; usually paired with "pacifying Tai Sui."
- Wealth Lamp (God of Wealth Lamp): for prosperity and thriving business, especially popular with businesspeople, salespeople, and stock traders, often set in the wealth-god hall.
- Wenchang Lamp: for exam luck and open wisdom, most often lit by students, and considered most potent at Wenchang Dijun temples (such as Taipei Wenchang Temple and Lukang's Wen Temple).
- Marriage Lamp: for a good match and romance luck, often lit by singles at Yue Lao temples; the one at Taipei's Xiahai City God Temple is the most famous.
- Medicine Buddha Lamp: for health and recovery from illness, most common at temples enshrining the Medicine Buddha.
- Peace Lamp: similar to the bright lamp, the name some temples use.

【Registration and Cost】
Registration usually opens from the twelfth to the first lunar month, covering the whole coming year (from the first day of the first month to New Year's Eve). You provide your full name, birth data (lunar year, month, day, and hour), and address, and the temple inscribes the lamp seat. Costs vary by temple, from a few hundred to a few thousand NT dollars. At famous temples the bright-lamp slots often can't meet demand -- big temples like Taipei Longshan Temple, Dajia Jenn Lann Temple, and Beigang Chaotian Temple frequently sell out before Lunar New Year, and some now open online registration.

【After Lighting a Lamp】
- A lit lamp doesn't mean all is well; you still have to strive and better yourself. As the folk saying goes, "Lighting a lamp is no match for accumulating virtue" -- a reminder that doing good is the true foundation.
- Some temples hold "fortune-mending" assemblies at the Lantern Festival, on the main deity's birthday, or on the first and fifteenth of each month, to bless those who have lit lamps.
- The lamp burns all year, and if it goes out midway the temple relights it. Most modern temples use LED bulbs in place of the old oil lamps -- safer, and less apt to go out.
- At year's end some temples hold a "thanking the lamp" rite, to thank the deity for a year's protection and to remind worshippers to renew for the coming year.
- If you light a lamp for a family member, it's best to get their consent first -- registration requires personal birth data, and some hold that it shouldn't be done on another's behalf without permission.

title: First Incense Race
summary: On Lunar New Year's Eve, at the stroke of midnight the bell rings, the temple doors fly open, and the waiting crowd surges in -- all to be first to plant their incense stick in the main burner. This is "grabbing the first incense," and believers hold that the year's very first stick of incense buys a whole year of good fortune.
content:
On Lunar New Year's Eve, as the midnight bell strikes twelve, the temple doors are flung wide and the crowd that has waited for hours pours in all at once, each racing to be the first to plant their incense stick in the great burner of the main hall -- the scene the news cameras never miss: grabbing the first incense.

【What the First Incense Means】
Tradition holds that whoever grabs the first incense receives the deity's earliest and most special blessing for the new year, luck riding high all the way through. But the first incense stands for more than luck -- it is devotion: a willingness to wait hours in the cold winter night just to be first to offer the deity a New Year prayer.

【Popular Temples for the First Incense】
- Taipei Longshan Temple: draws tens of thousands to queue each New Year's Eve, the grandest scene of all.
- Dajia Jenn Lann Temple, Taichung: central Taiwan's most popular spot, where Mazu devotees vie to pay their respects.
- Beigang Chaotian Temple: the south's most emblematic, with a long history of the first-incense tradition.
- Lukang Tianhou Temple: the New Year's Eve centerpiece of the old town of Lukang, wrapped in the festive air of its historic streets.
- Taipei Xingtian Temple: incense is banned here, yet devotees still vie to be the first worshipper of the new year.

【How Different Temples Do It】
The rules vary from temple to temple: some run a first-come sprint, worshippers dashing from the gate straight for the burner; others decide the first-incense honor by drawing lots or casting divination blocks, to avoid dangerous shoving; and some hand out numbered tickets first, then draw the first-incense guest from among the holders.

【Safety and the Modern Shift】
In recent years, for worshippers' safety, many temples have gradually reshaped the custom: swapping numbered tickets for the sprint, or choosing the first-incense guest by divination block, so a first-incense guest can emerge without the crush -- keeping the meaning of the tradition while looking after safety. Taipei Longshan Temple has simply had a temple representative plant the first incense at midnight on everyone's behalf.

【The New Year's Eve Temple Air】
In truth, first incense or not hardly matters -- a New Year's Eve visit to the temple is itself one of the most important New Year traditions for Taiwanese people. The temple hangs its lanterns and decorations, incense smoke drifting, as people arrive in new clothes with the whole family, young and old, to pray, receiving a temple-given "peace talisman" and "fortune money" to wish the new year well. However the form of grabbing the first incense may change, that prayer and hope for the new year has always been the warmest of Taiwanese festival memories.

title: Temple Visiting Guide
summary: Standing at the temple gate with three doors side by side -- which one do you walk through? And why must you never, ever step on the threshold? From "enter by the dragon gate, exit by the tiger gate" to worshipping Tiangong and the proper order of the halls, this guide walks the full temple worship flow so that every visit is respectful and fitting.
content:
You stand at the temple gate, three doors side by side -- do you know which one to take? And as you step through, why must that high threshold never be trodden on? Worshipping at a temple follows its own flow and etiquette, and getting the order right is not only respect for the deity but also lets the prayer in your heart ring more sincere.

【Entering the Gate】
Enter by the "dragon gate" (the right-hand door as you face the temple) and leave by the "tiger gate" (the left), following the auspicious sense of "enter the dragon gate, exit the tiger's mouth." The central "middle door" is the deity's own passage, not used by ordinary worshippers. Some modernized temples no longer keep the distinction strictly -- just follow the temple's guidance.

When stepping over the threshold, always lift your foot and step across; never tread on it. In folk belief the threshold stands for the deity's shoulders, and stepping on it is a grave irreverence -- one of the most important taboos in Taiwanese temple etiquette.

【The Order of Worship】
Once inside, the order of worship follows "outer to inner, center to sides, front to back":
1. The Tiangong censer (the burner at the very front of the temple): the first step on entering. Face outward (toward the heavens) and offer incense to Tiangong (the Jade Emperor). As supreme ruler of all deities, Tiangong is worshipped first, the highest mark of respect.
2. The main deity in the central hall: turn into the hall and offer incense to the temple's principal deity.
3. The dragon-side hall (the deity's left, as you face it): worship the dragon side first. In Chinese culture the dragon is honored and the tiger lowly, so the dragon side takes priority.
4. The tiger-side hall (the right): worship the tiger side next.
5. The rear hall: worship the deities of the rear hall last (often Guanyin or the Tai Sui star deities).

【Basic Etiquette】
- Dress neatly and modestly: nothing too revealing (no sleeveless tops, shorts, or flip-flops), and take special care in Buddhist temples.
- Keep quiet: a temple is a solemn religious place; no loud talk, no running or roughhousing.
- Photography: some temples or specific statues forbid photos, so ask the temple first; even where it's allowed, use no flash, and it's best to ask the deity silently before photographing a statue.
- Posture: press your palms together or hold incense, raise them to eyebrow height, and bow three times; when kneeling, both knees to the ground and the forehead lightly touching the cushion.
- Silent prayer: tell the deity your name, birth data, address, and request -- it needn't be long, but it should be sincere and specific.
- On leaving: before exiting by the tiger gate, you may turn to face the hall and bow, bidding the deity farewell as a final mark of respect.

【Special Reminders】
- Keep children safe inside a temple, well away from the burners and candle flames.
- Before bringing a pet, check whether the temple allows it.
- Temple volunteers are usually glad to explain the worship flow -- when unsure, just ask.

title: Worship Taboos
summary: Don't blow out the incense with your mouth, don't step on the threshold, and don't set a custard apple before the Buddha -- Taiwanese temples pass down many such taboos, and the versions vary from place to place. Learn these fine points and you can avoid an unwitting misstep, making every visit smoother and more complete.
content:
An incense stick nearly blown out by mouth, a foot about to land on the threshold, a custard apple casually set on the altar table -- in a Taiwanese temple, each of these makes people wince. Temple culture carries many taboos, and the versions differ from place to place; here are the most common ones -- remember them and you'll steer clear of an innocent misstep:

【Entering Taboos】
- Don't enter or leave by the middle door: it is the deity's passage; ordinary worshippers use the dragon or tiger gate.
- Don't step on the threshold: it stands for the deity's shoulders, and treading on it is a grave irreverence.
- Don't dress too revealingly: dress neatly and modestly for the temple, avoiding shorts, flip-flops, and skimpy clothing.

【Worship Taboos】
- Don't blow out the incense with your mouth: fan it out with your hand; blowing is seen as irreverent.
- Don't point the incense down or plant it carelessly: keep the incense pointing up, so your wish can rise to the heavens.
- Don't point at a deity statue with your finger: use your whole open hand as a mark of respect.
- Don't be noisy or rowdy in the hall: keeping solemn is basic etiquette.

【Offering Taboos】
- Don't offer tomato or guava to the gods: these two fruits have seeds that don't digest easily, carrying a sense of "uncleanness."
- Don't offer hollow-hearted things like water spinach: the "hollow heart" suggests "no sincere heart."
- Pineapple, apple, and orange are the most welcome, meaning "prosperity comes," "peace," and "good luck" respectively.
- Don't offer custard apple (sakya) to the Buddha: its name matches "Shakyamuni," and it's considered irreverent.

【Other Points】
- Traditionally, women avoided temples during menstruation -- but the origin of this custom lay mainly in the poor sanitation and nutrition of old times, when a woman's body was weaker during menstruation and a long trek to worship placed a real strain on it. With sanitation and medicine now vastly improved, most temples and religious figures agree there is no problem at all with visiting during menstruation; sincerity brings a response, and there's no need for such worry.
- It's best not to enter a temple straight after a funeral; purify yourself first, then go.
- Watch the incense fire for safety when bringing infants and young children into a temple.
- If you come across temple incense ash or a peace talisman, don't discard it casually; return it to the temple.

title: Consecration Ceremony (Kai Guang)
summary: A freshly carved deity statue is, in faith, still just a work of art -- until the ritual master's cinnabar brush dots in those eyes. Kai guang dian yan, "opening the light and dotting the eyes," is the crucial moment that infuses spiritual light into the statue and opens its divine gaze, so that from then on it can "see" the prayers of the faithful.
content:
A deity statue just finished, its face solemn and serene, is in matters of faith still only a "work of art" -- what truly turns it into a divinely empowered "golden body" is the instant the ritual master's cinnabar brush touches its eyes. This rite is called kai guang dian yan, "opening the light and dotting the eyes." A statue that has never been consecrated holds no spiritual power.

【The Meaning of Kai Guang】
"Kai guang" means "to open the light," symbolizing the infusion of spiritual radiance into the statue and the opening of its divine eyes, so that it may perceive the world and protect all beings. "Dian yan" -- dotting the eyes -- is the single most crucial step: the cinnabar brush touches the statue's eyes, symbolizing that the deity has opened its dharma-eyes and can from now on "see" the prayers of the faithful. The rite is usually presided over by a senior Taoist priest or an eminent Buddhist monk, and must fall on an auspicious day.

【Preparations Before Kai Guang】
- Choosing the day: an auspicious day is selected, usually by the ritual master according to the deity's attributes and the temple's needs.
- Installation (ru shen / zhuang zang): before the rite, "treasures" are placed inside a small cavity in the statue's back, a step called "installing the spirit." Common items include the five grains (rice, wheat, millet, sorghum, beans -- for abundance), gold and silver foil (wealth), cinnabar (warding off evil), talismans (protection), scriptures (blessing), and pearls and agate (auspicious energy). The cavity is then sealed with a wooden plug, signifying that the deity's spiritual power has been infused.
- Purifying the altar: the ritual master first performs a purification rite to cleanse the space and drive off unclean energy.

【The Kai Guang Dian Yan Ritual】
1. The ritual master, robed in his vestments, burns incense and chants scripture to invite the deity to descend.
2. With a cinnabar brush (or a writing brush dipped in cinnabar), he dots the statue's features in turn, reciting the matching incantation at each:
   - Eyes: "Dotting the eyes, the eyes see clear, able to behold all things of the world" -- so the deity may see the world's suffering.
   - Ears: "Dotting the ears, the ears hear keen, able to heed the faithful of all directions" -- so the deity may hear the worshippers' prayers.
   - Nose: "Dotting the nose, the nose discerns true, able to tell good from evil" -- so the deity may distinguish right from wrong.
   - Mouth: "Dotting the mouth, the mouth speaks wise, able to preach and guide all beings" -- so the deity may teach and transform.
   - Forehead: "Dotting the forehead, the forehead shines bright, able to light up the world" -- so the deity's wisdom may illuminate the world.
   - Hands: "Dotting the hands, the hands work strong, able to save the people from fire and flood" -- so the deity may extend its saving power.
   - Feet: "Dotting the feet, the feet stride firm, able to patrol and watch all lands" -- so the deity may make its rounds of the four directions.
3. Finally, a mirror (symbolizing light) is used to reflect over the whole statue, signifying that the illumination is complete.
4. Firecrackers sound together to announce that the kai guang is done, and the statue has officially become a "divided-spirit golden body" of the deity.

【Enthronement and Procession】
Once the kai guang is complete, the statue is "enthroned" (an zuo) -- set in its proper place in the temple or the home shrine, with a formal dharma assembly. For the consecration of an important deity, the temple will often also hold a "procession" (rao jing), letting the newly consecrated statue tour its jurisdiction and receive the worship of the faithful.

【Things to Note】
- Kai guang is an irreversible sacred rite; once done, the statue is regarded as a divided spirit of the deity and must never be carelessly discarded or damaged.
- If a home statue is damaged and needs replacing, the old one should be returned to a temple for a "de-consecration" (tui shen) rite before proper disposal.
- When watching a kai guang ceremony, keep quiet and reverent -- no loud noise or improper behavior.
